speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege. This question of privilege is twofold. It arises as a consequence of the fourth report of the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections which appears in Votes and Proceedings for last Thursday.
One of the main considerations of that committee was the question of qualifications of electors and candidates in elections. I had presented a bill, C-120, similar to a bill which had been presented by the Minister without Portfolio from York-Scarborough and to two other bills which were on the Order Paper. All these bills, which were referred to the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections, provided that all people who vote in elections or who are candidates in elections should be Canadian citizens. The idea was that the Canada Elections Act would be changed so that British subjects who were not Canadian citizens would no longer be entitled to vote in elections or be candidates in an election.
Apparently this matter was considered by the Committee on Privileges and Elections and in its fourth report under item 9 of Part I of the recommendations the sense of those bills has been completely reversed. It states in effect that only Canadian citizens would be qualified as electors and then in parentheses these words are added:
for this purpose British subjects, other than Canadian citizens, who were ordinarily resident in Canada on the 25th day of June 19G7, be deemed to be Canadian citizens.
Mr. Speaker, one cannot be deemed to be a Canadian citizen. Either one is a Canadian citizen or is not. This whole thing is a mockery of the bills that were referred to the committee. Under the guise of saying that one must be a Canadian citizen in order to qualify as an elector the committee has added in parentheses that a British subject is to be deemed to be a Canadian citizen.

May I first thank the hon. member for his co-operation in agreeing yesterday to postpone the consideration of this matter until this sitting of the House. The delay has made it possible to give additional consideration to the interesting point he has raised for determination by the Chair. The hon. member reminded the House that Bill C-120 standing in the hon. member's name was removed from the Order Paper some time ago after the subject matter thereof was referred by consent, to the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections. Eventually, the committee reported to the House. The committee report does refer to the hon. member's bill and submits recommendations which the hon. member suggests differ from the proposals contained in his bill.
The hon. member suggests that he has a question of privilege on two counts: first, that the committee report does not conform with certain aspects of his private bill and, second,
March 24, 1970

Treatment of Private Bills that he was not notified when the committee proceeded with the consideration of Bill C-120.
I wish I could say that as a result of the additional time I have had to consider this matter, due to the hon. member's forbearance and courtesy, the Chair has been able to conclude that he has a legitimate question of privilege. In my view, whether the committee's findings and recommendations conform or do not conform with the proposals contained in the private bill cannot constitute a question of privilege. There are no rules and no precedents to support the hon. member's contention.
The second difficulty raised by the hon. member for Cochrane to the effect that he did not receive advance notice of the consideration by the committee of the subject matter of the bill, while it may amount to a legitimate grievance, does not justify a prima facie question of privilege. All hon. members will agree, I am sure, that as a matter of courtesy an hon. member whose bill or motion is to be considered by a committee should be notified by the committee chairman, the committee clerk, or someone on their behalf. I believe that this is the normal practice. I believe that in normal circumstances, when a private bill, or more often the subject matter of a private bill, is referred for consideration by a committee, either the committee chairman or the committee clerk gets in touch with the member or the member himself takes the initiative to communicate with the officers in charge of proceedings in the committee to ensure that he will be available when the matter is considered and discussed in the committee. In any event I would like to suggest that the procedure should be reviewed so as to ensure that advance notice is always conveyed to the sponsors of private bills and resolutions which have been referred to committees so that the unfortunate incident of which the hon. member has been a victim cannot be repeated.
This having been said, I have to rule that although the hon. member would appear to have a very legitimate grievance, there is no question of privilege on which a motion could be founded and put to the House at this time.

Mr. Speaker, pursuant to Standing Order 17 I rise on a question of privilege. Notice of this question has been given to Your Honour to fulfil the conditions of Standing Order 17(2). My ques-

tion of privilege relates to the mail addressed to, and I quote, "My Member of Parliament, P.O. Box 4430, Ottawa, Ontario."
I raise this question at the earliest opportunity because it has only come to my attention that mail intended for myself was forwarded to another Member of Parliament, and because of other details regarding this case of which I was not aware prior to now.
I believe that Members of Parliament have the right to expect free access by their constituents to themselves without going through an outside intermediary, and I maintain that the action taken by those responsible for the dissemination of information indicating an improper address for Members of Parliament is a direct violation of my privileges and the privileges of all members of this House.

maintopic: MR. CAFIK-USE OF POST OFFICE BOX 4430

maintopic: MR. CAFIK-USE OF POST OFFICE BOX 4430
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as much as I laud the actions of those responsible for these advertisements in so far as they are attempting to involve more people in the democratic process and to advance the goal of participation in the Governmental Process, I feel that their ill-conceived actions have resulted in a backward step for genuine participation. It does not further the cause of participation to publish a misleading and erroneous address for all members of this House.
I further contend that no individuals or groups have the right, however lofty their motives, to place themselves as an intermediary between the public and their elected representatives, and to do so is to violate our exclusive rights as members of this House.

maintopic: MR. CAFIK-USE OF POST OFFICE BOX 4430
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: MR. CAFIK-USE OF POST OFFICE BOX 4430
speechtext:
I further contend that no one has the right to intercept my mail and remove it from the post office for any purpose whatsoever. This is not only a violation of the Post Office Act, section 8, which gives the Postmaster General the sole and exclusive privilege of collecting, conveying and delivering letters within Canada, but it is also a violation of the privileges of this House in so far as this mail was directed to Members of Parliament. Furthermore, the Post Office Act, section 39, indicates that "mailable matter becomes the property of the person to whom it is addressed when deposited in a post office."
I further contend that the very act of establishing this post office box is a contravention of my rights as a member of this House and the Post Office Act, section 69, which makes it
March 24, 1970

an offence for anyone other than the postal authorities to "undertake to collect, convey or deliver any letter within Canada."
It is my understanding, Mr. Speaker, that not only was this mail removed from the post office box but that in many cases such mail was redirected to Members of Parliament on an arbitrary basis without due consideration to determine to whom it should have been directed. Consequently mail intended for one Member of Parliament was misdirected to other Members of Parliament.
I believe, Mr. Speaker, that all hon. members have the right to know what happened to this mail following its removal from post office box 4430 and prior to it being delivered. Were tabulations prepared as to quantity, or was any attempt made to prepare mailing lists? If either of these things was done I feel, with all respect, that our rights have been most seriously violated.

To start with, I suggest that this attempt to legislate by use of an estimate is most improper and should not be permitted.
Even more at fault, however, is the attempt by the committee to vary the original vote in two very material respects. In permitting this, we get away from the very wholesome restraints which the exercise of the legislative process permits us. I am amazed at what has happened here. I do not want to go into it to any extent, but certainly there must be some fault on the part of the Treasury or of the Minister without Portfolio who has been handling the particular item under discussion, namely, vote 17b which appears on page 2 of the supplementary estimates of the Department of Agriculture.
This attempt to short circuit the normal legislative process by legislating by means of a vote is wrong, but it is even more wrong to attempt to vary the result later. However, I will deal with that later since it is a question of substance. Now, I just want to stake out my claim.
What we are faced with now is the fact that the Committee on Miscellaneous Estimates purported to change in two very material respects the original vote 17b in the supplementary estimates of the Department of Agriculture. In the first instance, what was done was to change the category of persons entitled to receive the grants from those who were described as holders of permit books under the Wheat Board Act to people who are producers.
Obviously, we are referring to the Wheat Board Act, but I will not take up the time of the House by quoting from it. However, there is no question that a producer is not necessarily the same as a holder of a permit book under the Wheat Board Act. Obviously, those who hold permit books must be producers, but producers need not necessarily be holders of these permits. The words, "providing for a board of appeal to determine disputes hereunder" were added by the committee to the wording of the vote. These words do not appear in the original vote, and constitute a very substantial alteration of the purposes of the original vote as brought down with the message of His Excellency, and contained in the supplementary estimates. I would suggest 
that under those circumstances there is no question but that this House should not consider the amended vote in the business of supply.
However, Mr. Speaker, because this is a very serious issue I would like to ask very briefly, what are the rights of committees in this regard? I would not ask Your Honour to make a judgment at this time covering what should be the terms and conditions with regard to committees in the future but we must remember, Sir, and I think the House should remember, that we have embarked on a completely new procedure. It could be a very excellent procedure, but we must remember we have taken out from this House the old committee of supply procedure, under which there was the right to have a careful examination of estimates and the ability to move amendments. This right has been taken away, and in the result we have put into the hands of committees the right to deal with these estimates.
Now, Mr. Speaker, what limitation should be placed on these committees, bearing in mind that in the period from 1958 to 1962, some 55, 60 and 65 days were often taken by some of the eminent members of the opposition at that time in their examination of the estimates. Are the committees to be limited to the simple right to say yes or no in dealing with these estimates? Are committees possibly to have the right-this is what I would ask Your Honour to consider because committees are now involved in dealing with these estimates-to add recommendations urging the House to consider what steps can be taken, whether by a humble message to His Excellency or by a simple recommendation, to ask for permission to vary the purpose of votes or to extend the amounts?
I have been in touch with members of various committees who are disturbed over the question of what are and what are not then-rights in this regard. I do not expect Your Honour, on this rather narrow point which now confronts you, to make a decision on the wider aspect which I have asked you to consider. However, I hope that during the period of the Easter Recess Your Honour would give some consideration to this, and by a proposal to the Committee on Procedure and Organization, or by a statement in this House, be of some help to the Standing Committees that will be dealing with these estimates after the recess. I shall have something more to say after we get into the actual business of

I thank hon. members for their views. The fact that there is unanimity among those who have participated in the procedural discussion makes it easier for the Chair. In fact, for a moment, I wondered whether there was any point in giving a decision but I think it is probably wise to make a ruling based on the advice of hon. members who have taken part in the discussion and who have agreed on a conclusion. As hon. members know, the procedural point was raised last Friday and I indicated then that I had serious misgivings about the procedural aspects of this matter. I have had an opportunity to review it since then and my conclusions coincide with those we have heard during the last few minutes from the hon. members who have taken part in this discussion. It is hardly necessary to remind hon. members that paragraph 1 of the Fourth Report of the Standing Committee on Miscellaneous Estimates reads in part as follows:
Delete in vote 17b, on page 2, the paragraph intituled "Grants", and substitute the following therefor:
The report goes on to rewrite in substantial manner vote 17b of the supplementary estimates (B). It is not necessary, I suggest, to compare in detail the terms of the committee's proposed recommendation with that of the original estimate to establish the fact that a change of substance has been suggested by the committee. In its recommendations, the committee has proposed an alternative to the proposal recommended to the House by His Excellency. No principle is more surely provided for by our constitution and our Standing Orders than that which provides that the Crown alone initiates financial proposals.

In this regard, section (1) of Standing Order 62 reads as follows:
This House shall not adopt or pass any vote, resolution, address or bill for the appropriation of any part of the public revenue, or of any tax or impost, to any purpose that has not been first recommended to the House by a message from the Governor General in the session in which such vote, resolution, address or bill is proposed.
In the same regard, section (3) of citation 246 of Beauchesne's fourth edition reads as follows:
The guiding principle in determining the effect of an amendment upon the financial initiative of the Crown is that the communication, to which the royal demand of recommendation is attached, must be treated as laying down once and for all (unless withdrawn and replaced) not only the amount of a charge, but also its objects, purposes, conditions and qualifications. In relation to the standard thereby fixed, an amendment infringes the financial initiative of the Crown, not only if it increases the amount, but also if it extends the objects and purposes, or relaxes the conditions and qualifications expressed in the communication by which the Crown has demanded or recommended a charge. And this standard is binding not only on private members but also on ministers whose only advantage is that, as advisors of the Crown, they can present new or supplementary estimates or secure the royal recommendation to new or supplementary resolutions.
Along the same vein, may I refer to section (3) of citation 244 of Beauchesne's, as follows:
Amendments proposing, in a money resolution, to substitute a loan for a subsidy; to change the destination, purpose and conditions of a subsidy: attaching a condition to a subsidy; affecting the ends and provisions of a subsidy, must be moved by a minister with the recommendation of the Crown.
There are a number of other citations that can be brought to bear on the same question, but I do not think it will be necessary for me to do so at this stage. It is not competent, I suggest, for the House or any committee of this House to substitute a financial provision in an estimate for one which has been recommended by His Excellency.
For the foregoing reasons, I must decide that the report of the Standing Committee on Miscellaneous Estimates presented to the House Thursday, March 19th last, is a nullity and that no subsequent proceeding may or need be taken in relation thereto.
In view of this decision I assume hon. members will want to give thought to the suggestion made by the President of the Privy Council, although the request would have to be made, I assume, by the President of the Treasury Board.

Mr. Speaker, as I understand it, we are now permitted to make general remarks on

programs of the government. I wish to take this opportunity to speak briefly about matters that were under very heavy discussion last week, specifically inflation and unemployment, and what the government's programs have done to make these situations considerably worse.
A week ago Sunday night, all of those who were watching the CBC television news were very surprised to hear the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) disclose the latest chapter in the government's four year effort to curb inflation. At that time the final plans of his government, which claims to be a modern government using computers and a lot of bright young men who fill the Prime Minister's office called modern thinkers, was disclosed.
We were amazed to hear the Minister of Finance, in his disclosure of the government's present plans to curb inflation, disclose a plan that has been in operation in various countries throughout the world for literally hundreds of years. This government of computers and bright young men is now going to fight inflation by that age old process of slowing down the economy by restricting credit. That has always been followed in every country where it has been tried by workers being laid off. When they get hungry, these workers are willing to work for less. This brings costs down, prices fall and the country concerned considers that it has licked inflation.
We heard the Minister of Finance say very clearly on television the other night that this government considers it may be necessary to have higher unemployment in 1970 than it had in 1969, if, in his own words, we are really going to lick inflation. So there you have the policy of this government. After four years of failure in its efforts to curb inflation it is finally going back to policies that have been in operation for hundreds of years. It is finally admitting that the best the so-called just society can produce is that great reactionary and harsh policy of growing unemployment, growing misery and growing hardship, which has been in use for so long.
Let us examine for a moment this government's programs for fighting inflation in the past four years. During the first three of those four years it resorted, in various budgets, to increasing taxes, which did not work. The cost of living kept increasing year by year at a steadily accelerating rate. Finally, after three years of increased taxes the government decided this method was not effective.
March 24, 1970

Then, last June the government tried another method of fighting inflation. The Minister of Finance told us that the government plan consisted of slowing down construction over the next two years in the three most wealthy provinces, Ontario, Alberta and British Columbia, by withholding the 5 per cent capital cost allowance to builders in order to persuade them not to build for the next two years. The government forgot to take one important matter into consideration. The builders knew very well that building costs in Canada were going up at a rate of 12 per cent per year. Through a very simple process of arithmetic they knew that if they put off building for two years and started again two years later it would cost them 24 per cent more to build the same building at that time than it would today. They decided this was not good business, that is to increase costs in two years by about 25 per cent in order to save 5 per cent for two years. So, the builders simply laughed at the government and went right on building. That program proved completely worthless.
The other program the Minister of Finance announced last June was equally ineffective. He told us on the night he presented his budget that the Kennedy Round tariff reductions, which were originally supposed to be spread over the next three years, would become effective that very night. He said this lowering of tariffs on a great number of items would increase competition in Canada and lower the price of goods, thereby slowing down the increase in the cost of living and the rapidly rising inflation.
Once again, the government forgot one very important factor. It did not have any way available to require importers to pass on the savings to the consumer. I refer to the savings resulting from removing the tariffs. So the importers did exactly what the builders did. They simply laughed at the government. They did not pass along the tariff reductions; prices did not come down, prices kept going up at an ever-increasing rate. Once again all importers, as has been the case in respect of the construction men, simply laughed at the government.

Neither is good for the maintenance of the respect a government should receive from the people of the country. The people in the business community know this government is not a business government. Mr. Speaker, the answer is that this government is run by four men who, by no stretch of the imagination, are businessmen.
These four men are the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), the Secretary of State (Mr. Pelletier), the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Marchand) and the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Pepin). These gentlemen are very nice men to meet and are charming men to whom to talk. In their own fields, I am sure they are very good and were very good before they entered government. Three were professors and one was a labour leader. I am sure they all did their jobs extremely well in the fields in which they were. But these men do not understand plain, ordinary business principles. These are the men who decide what the government is and is not to do. This is not done in an official way. This is the type of consultation that is carried on in any government by a group, usually of five, six or seven persons, which controls the government. These are the men in the government who quietly decide the direction in which the government is to move. This is not done officially. It is just one of the things that happen in every government.
These four men who run this government do not happen to be businessmen. They do not understand business practices. This proposal affects the livelihood of approximately 190,000 permit holders in western Canada. It is one thing to pass legislation which would permit these people to either take advantage of such a program or stay out of it, but it is another thing to propose a plan which does not give this large number of farmers a real choice. This is the point at which this bill goes past the ordinary prerogatives of the government. The government may have advisers who think that they have within themselves the knowledge to plan production on the individual farms in western Canada and to tell the individual farmer what he may or may not do. They propose to send inspectors to his farm to see that he does what he is supposed to do, and to see that he does it in the way in which it is supposed to be done. But I suggest that any department or any group of men or women who think they can undertake such a task are indeed taking a great deal upon themselves.

In all conscience, to make economic or moral sense, the people of that region have a right to know where they are heading. Above all else the farmer is a planner. He has to be a planner. What farmers do next year is planned with what they are going to do the year after that in mind. If you are going to put in forage, then obviously you

Its program covers just one year. In our mythology we say that Saskatchewan is a next year country. Above all, the minister should know this. Admittedly he is not a farmer himself, but you do not have to be a farmer to acquire the wisdom to know what happens. Surely, he ought to know that this is a next year country.

Here we have this program purporting to put $100 million-odd dollars into the hands of farmers but nobody knows how much of it will actually get there. If it does get there the farmer will probably spend most of it trying to conform with the non-productive program which the government has dreamed up. The only advice I can give to the minister and those around him is to adjust the program before it is too late. Try to recapture some of the confidence of the farmers, try to get them to work along with you to achieve some possible objective. Try for a program which will improve the condition of the farmer and not add to his difficulties.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to speak in this debate I wish to make a few brief remarks about matters that concern my riding, my province and the nation generally. About two weeks ago we heard the budget speech presented in the House by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson). The budget speech confirmed what hon. members on this side of the House and the Canadian public have been thinking for the past couple of years, that there is now a 21774-65
DEBATES	5421
Supplementary Estimates new meaning to the old Liberal slogan, "participatory democracy". That meaning is summed up by the phrase, "sharing the grief".
While the Minister of Finance arrogantly balances himself on the edge of his House of Commons seat, almost 6 million Canadians living below the poverty line are trying to balance themselves on their meagre budgets and keep body and soul together on salaries which fall below the poverty level.
Much has been said of the present government and the fact that it was elected on the charisma of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau); he made no promises, except that he would build a just society. He did not keep that promise. He built an unjust society. It is equally obvious the government is anxious to keep the Prime Minister's latest promise to force the unemployment rate in Canada up to 6 per cent. According to the latest statistics released by the Dominion Bureau of Statistics, the unemployment rate as a national average is 6.5 per cent of our labour force. In the Atlantic provinces the rate has been forced-and I use the word "forced" deliberately, because the policies of the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance have forced up the unemployment rate in Atlantic Canada-to 11 per cent.
In the absence of definite figures for Newfoundland, I predict that the unemployment rate there will probably exceed 20 per cent. When one realizes that one fifth of wage earners of a province of Canada will be unemployed, should not one be frightened? One ought to be alarmed at the 6.5 per cent national unemployment rate, the highest in six or seven years. Since assuming office in 1968, this government has embarked on a deliberate policy of forcing people onto the rolls of the unemployed. That is no laughing matter. The average unemployed Canadian must now be asking himself, "What is this all about and where will it end." Having spoken to the people of my riding, of my province generally and to other Canadians, I am convinced our people realize that the government does not know where it is going and what is worst they could not care less. The answer to the second part of the question, "Where will it all end," will be found in the ballot boxes after the next general election.
The government has embarked on a policy that is rapidly strangling the Canadian economy. Certainly, it has a stranglehold on the unemployed, on those living below the poverty line, on western farmers, Atlantic fishermen, small businessmen and Canadians gen-

March 24, 1970
Supplementary Estimates erally. Its callous and indifferent attitude towards the economically depressed regions of Canada is sapping the spirit and initiative of our people, and in my opinion can only result in social and economic disaster. The government refuses to acknowledge that our economy is on its knees and actually bleeding to death. The Minister of Finance, his colleagues and the Prime Minister go about their merry way arrogantly boasting about the rapidly increasing unemployment rate and their phoney war on inflation.
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
At the same time, they have the gall to brag about how generous they are towards the depressed, have-not areas of Canada. Let the Prime Minister and Minister of Finance convince the unemployed in this country and those living below the poverty line that the government's anti-inflation policy is the right one. Let them try to convince the 83,000 Newfoundlanders who have been forced to accept welfare that the government's anti-inflation policy is the right one. The figure to which I referred a moment ago with regard to unemployment must give the Prime Minister a great deal of satisfaction.
This government appears to have adopted the attitude of "don't confuse us with the facts". The fact is that those regions of the country which do not contribute to inflation, such as the Atlantic provinces and Quebec, are being forced to take the same medicine as the wealthier provinces where there may be a need to impose anti-inflationary measures.
It is obvious there is a great deal of confusion in the government. In my two years as a member I have witnessed the Minister of Fisheries and Forestry (Mr. Davis) and the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Laing) continually battling the question of what comes first, the fishermen or necessary facilities for fishermen? This is similar to the question which came first, the chicken or the egg? I know in my constituency many people wish to return to the fishing industry but are unable to do so because of a lack of adequate facilities. The Minister of Public Works has refused to approve expenditures to build facilities because there are no fishermen in the area. He does not recognize the fact that these people are not actively engaged in the fisheries because there are no facilities. That is why I say they are arguing about what comes first, fishermen or facilities.
There have been a number of developments in recent months which are having a detri-

mental effect on the economy in the have-not areas. I do not want to drag out the subject of the seal fishery, but what my colleagues have said in this House bears repeating. Regulations have been imposed by the Minister of Fisheries, the basis of which stem almost entirely from the fact there have been representations by our embassies in Europe and other parts of the world because of pressure applied to them by the so-called sob-sisters, the bleeding heart societies and, in many cases, the vested interests. Our government has seen fit to yield to the pressure applied by those people at the expense of the Atlantic coast fishermen who, in many cases, augment their income from the seal fishery. Because of the regulations now imposed, it will be extremely difficult for these fishermen. There are fishermen in Atlantic Canada who desperately need the extra few dollars available from the seal fishery.
This government, with its typical arrogance and lack of interest or concern for the have-nots of this nation, has set about to destroy that industry. They have robbed those fishermen of the chance to earn a few dollars to tide them over until they return to their fishing boats or engage in some other job. I believe these regulations are crazy and stupid. They certainly were not well thought out by the Minister of Fisheries or his staff. Any reasonable person who has any idea of what is happening in Atlantic Canada would never allow this sort of thing. The Minister of Fisheries has done a great deal for the fisheries of Atlantic Canada. I am surprised that he permitted this regulation to be imposed on the sealing industry. It will have a ruinous effect on the industry, if not this year then next year or the year after.
The Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Marchand) recently made a statement boasting of the fact that there were 22 areas in Canada designated to be special areas. There are eight such areas in Newfoundland. One area in my riding which is certainly more deserving than probably any other part of the province, was not even mentioned. I refer to the Argentia-Placentia area and the phasing out of the Argentia US naval station. There are approximately 200 fishermen and their families who were resettled in that area by this government and the Newfoundland government. They have not been provided with any facilities to encourage them to earn a living from the fisheries. It is a very depressed area. I am very disappointed that the minister did not see fit to extend the
March 24, 1970

same benefits to that area that will be extended to other specially designated areas in Canada.
In that same area there is a great deal of economic and social unrest as well as uncertainty, brought about by the government's resettlement program. I have said before in this House and in committee, and I will keep saying that there has been a grave injustice done to the people who were encouraged and in some cases forced to vacate their former homes and properties to move to the so-called resettlement areas. These people were enticed to move by the government. They were helped financially to a certain extent to help defray the cost of moving and to resettle. They were then completely forgotten.
These people were treated like checkers on a board, like pieces of machinery, like little red pins on a map. They were taken away from the place their families had been for generations, in most cases in areas where they could earn a decent living for themselves and their families. In some cases, they were forced to move to the so-called growth areas. They now find they are completely incapable of carrying on their vocation of fishing. They have been almost forced to become welfare addicts. I believe this is a serious injustice.
I hope this government will recognize its responsibility and pay special attention to the people concerned. The government should help them to rehabilitate themselves in their new environment. These people should be given a chance to restore their independence. Like most Canadians, they want to be able to stand tall, walk straight and earn a decent living for themselves and their families. I have spent hours talking about this, written hundreds of letters and have made many speeches on the subject. Much to my regret and the regret of the people concerned, the government so far has elected to turn a deaf ear to the problem. Special attention should be given to these areas by the Department of Regional Economic Expansion in view of the fact their way of life was destroyed by the government and they are now unable to help themselves. As I said a moment ago, they are unable to earn a living for themselves and their families.
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
There are a number of other matters which affect my area, one of which is housing. I was very interested in the question asked today by the hon. member for Prince Edward-Has-tings (Mr. Hees). He challenged the Prime
21774-65J
Supplementary Estimates Minister to pay some attention and visit the slums of Canada in the same way which he did in the Arctic. As the hon. member mentioned later, this is not a popular suggestion because slums do not make good pictures. I would also challenge the Prime Minister and the minister responsible for housing to go into parts of my riding where people are living under conditions which are altogether substandard, and should not to be tolerated by anyone in 1970. The government does not seem to appreciate the need for decent housing which exists among Canadians. Hon. gentlemen opposite are making a lot of noise about urban renewal schemes and subsidized housing, but not enough is being done in an area which should obviously be given priority. I urge the government to step up its programs in this field. There is great need for urban renewal in Canada. There is great need for extensive studies to ascertain the fact of bad housing conditions, with their attendant inconvenience and squalor, and the effect it is having upon our young people who will be governing Canada tomorrow. Again, I urge the government to intensify its program to enable those now experiencing wretched-substandard housing conditions to enjoy some of the amenities that are being taken for granted by most Canadians.

speechtext:
On rising to speak on this bill, may I say that I intend to confine my comments to the subject of the Lift program announced by the minister in charge of the Wheat Board. I do not know how well this program has been named; I strongly suspect there is not much lift attached to this program and that it may never get off the ground. In some respects this is a pity, because it might have been a useful program. But it was ill-conceived and ill-considered; the most charitable thing one could say about it, I suppose, is that it was introduced in too great a hurry.
During his budget speech the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) told us that it would be necessary to introduce supplementary estimates providing $100 million for prairie farmers. The Lift program will certainly not need all that money. Upwards of half of it will be saved, unless all the reports I have received are misleading. I say from personal knowledge, and as a result of discussions with farmers and with hon. members of this House who come from agricultural areas, that it will be virtually impossible for farmers to follow this plan in its entirety.

March 24. 1970
Supplementary Estimates
The prediction in the Richardson Grain Letter that the figure of 15 million acres would be realized seems to be altogether optimistic. Reports indicate that the plan will have minimal acceptance in Manitoba and Alberta, and perhaps more effect in the great wheat lands of Saskatchewan. Statistics from the Dominion Bureau indicate that farmers will be planting about 18 million acres. If a figure of 15 million is realized, it means a net reduction of seven million acres.
The minister's plan to divert 20 million acres to summerfallow and two million acres to forage appear unrealistic and lacking in foresight. My criticism does not apply so strongly to the proposal relating to forage; that seems to be a useful program. The scheme as a whole would get rid of wheat, but at enormous cost. Because of the way in which surplus wheat is distributed all over the prairies, many farmers would still have very little to sell, while others will be left with a great deal. As the scheme was outlined by the minister, a farmer would receive payment for putting his land to summerfallow or forage, and be allocated a quota for delivering wheat, the quota being related to wheat he does not grow.
The second half of the program is, thus, attractive only to farmers who have sizeable surpluses of wheat on their farms. Their number is hard to assess but it seems likely it will amount to about 50 per cent, and to somewhat more in Saskatchewan. Farmers who have little wheat in stock would do best to try to grow a substantial crop on a small acreage. This is what often happens when an attempt is made to reduce acreage; farmers cultivate more intensively and end up with almost as many bushels as before. As a number of hon. members have pointed out, the plan tends to penalize farmers who have reduced their acreage in the past few years of their own accord.
I wish to turn, now, to a facet of the minister's announcement which seems to have escaped attention. All the announcements refer to an eight bushel quota. The minister did say the figure could be nine bushels if the maximum summerfallow came into being and no wheat were grown at all. In this respect he would seem to be on very safe ground, since some 50 per cent of farmers have no carryover-though it is true they may be farming a smaller number of acres than the 50 per cent which hold a surplus.
Nowhere in the Lift program or in the minister's statements is the Wheat Board

committed to taking more than eight bushels. However one tries to work out a quota to fit this new program, it seems the government is not committed to taking into the grain handling system more than about 300 million bushels of wheat. On the basis of 30 million acres of summerfallow this year, plus two million acres under forage crops, plus 25 per cent of last year's summerfallow, making up about 39 million acres of eligible quota acres, the amount of grain which can be delivered would total about 300 million bushels to reach an eight bushel per specified acreage quota. Four various reasons, though, many farmers would obviously not have the amount of wheat necessary if the full quota is to be reached. Even if the acreage under summerfallow were increased and wheat acreage reduced, there would still be less wheat delivered under the quota because many farmers would lack the wheat to fill their quotas if they reduced their acreage.
What about disappearances from the system? The minister has stated that this year 375 million bushels would disappear into export channels. Taking into account a further 100 million or 150 million flowing into domestic channels, there could be a total disappearance from the system of some 500 million bushels. But the Wheat Board is committed to taking only 300 million bushels of wheat, so there could be a loss from stocks of about 200 million bushels currently held by the Board. This would be a good thing for the government but it would really amount to transferring the burden to the farmer.
[DOT] (5.30 p.m.)
The really serious impact of this policy will be to reduce the cash flow to the grain farmers, computed on the basis of $1.25 a bushel for 200 million bushels, by about $250 million even at today's reduced prices. This would be nothing short of an economic disaster for the western grain farmer and indeed the whole grain economy throughout the country, particularly if this policy is carried out as bluntly as is suggested.
Even if two million acres of forage are put into crops and another six million in summerfallow more than last year, the government would contribute only $50 million to $55 million to the farm economy. Unless the government is committed to taking more than 300 million bushels into export and domestic systems, it seems to me the western farmer is in for a severe blow which will be felt throughout the entire western economy.
March 24, 1970

I should now like to turn to a more serious matter in its impact, at least in many ways- the new use of quotas to restrict deliveries. The government has proceeded in this matter by regulation, though many people still feel it should have been done by legislation. After all, this is a drastic change in the whole pattern of grain marketing and there has been no opportunity for debate on this important matter and no opportunity for the elected representatives of farming groups and other interested parties to appear before a parliamentary committee such as the Committee on Agriculture. This is what we would normally expect. It would seem that voluntary action might have been obtained with the same results.
The new regulations carry a very large stick indeed, since the producer's deliveries will be restricted if he fails to utilize his land in a fashion approved by the government. I should like to quote from an editorial which appeared in the Winnipeg Free Press of March 20 under the title "Is it legal?" It refers to the regulatory powers of the act and states in part:
But it is certainly not self-evident that there is any such power in the act. One looks for it in vain in article 4, which sets out the board's specific powers; for example; "to buy, take delivery or, store, transfer, sell, ship or otherwise dispose of grain"-
It goes on:
These obviously are marketing powers. There are a pair of basket clauses at the end empowering the board to act as an agent on behalf of a minister or the government "in respect of any operations that it may be directed to carry out by the Governor in Council" and "generally to do all such acts and things as may be necessary or incidental to carrying out its operations."
It continues:
Obviously an acreage reduction program cannot be classified as an "incidental" and it has not been "necessary" in more than three decades of Wheat Board experience. The preceding language is presumably to be read in the context of the whole act. At face value there would be no limit to what the board could do on government direction, but this would be a nonsensical construction. In fact the act has to do with marketing and it is certainly arguable that production is a quite different subject.
Other sections of the statute, for example those dealing with permit books and powers of administration, appear no more helpful. Even the definition of quota looks difficult; it means "the quantity of grain described in a permit book as fixed from time to time by the board." How is "grain produced" to be equated with summer-fallow or, for that matter, forage? While it is beyond question that the board's powers over marketing, as established by past cases, are very extensive, the presumption that they are ample
Supplementary Estimates enough to permit it to alter production patterns under threat of penalty certainly invites serious challenge.
Regulations ought not to have a retroactive effect. A farmer who summerfallowed land last year voluntarily is automatically being penalized by some loss of his quota entitlement. There is no escape from the penalty which is inherent in the quota, and the penalty is a matter of regulation and not of legislation passed by Parliament.
Further on the editorial states:
In this case 188,000 producers, who were obviously not consulted as individuals, have been suddenly confronted with a requirement that they alter their whole scheme of production. Quantitative changes in quotas are, of course, usual but in this instance the whole basis of establishing quotas has been changed overnight from the practice of three decades.
So the workings of this act or regulation, which might have produced a useful effort, will not contribute much toward the reduction of grain without a serious loss of income and damage to the western grain economy. This program seems to have been devised hurriedly, and with little thought, by people who are not fully conversant with the needs of the western farmers. In concluding these few remarks, I urge the minister to withdraw or make major changes to this program. It might be a useful program, but I suggest that the problem of surplus wheat can be solved only by selling. We cannot in one year curtail the production of western grain to the extent that we will end up with little or no surplus. I sincerely hope the minister will take a good look at what he has proposed and make some very useful changes.

subtopic: BUSINESS OF SUPPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to take part in this debate on the supplementary estimates and to deal further with a matter my colleague, the hon. member for Saskatoon-Biggar (Mr. Gleave), initially brought to the attention of the House. The hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Ritchie) has spoken on it, and I expect one or two more hon. members will deal with this matter when I have concluded my remarks.
For anyone to suggest that this so-called Operation Lift-I believe the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Korchinski) had different words for it, and I have regarded it as "Liberals Increasing Farmers' Troubles"-is being approved and accepted by anything more than half the farmers in western Canada, let alone the majority, is to indicate that he is suffering from delusions of some kind.

March 24, 1970
Supplementary Estimates
In true Liberal fashion the minister has dubbed and clubbed his hasty wheat acreage reduction plan as Operation Lift. It would be more appropriate, I think, to use the initials of the plan itself, WARP or operation WARP. My dictionary gives the following definition of warp: to change from straight or right or natural state; to make crooked or perverted. That is a pretty good definition of what this plan will do to Prairie farming. The minister laboured "Lang," or long, and concluded that we would have less wheat in 1970 if we did not grow any wheat in 1970. This was his conclusion after all that labour.
The Liberals have been somewhat less than honest in their promotion of operation WARP. They have implied that it will provide a large income supplement to grain growers. In the minister's words, "If farmers get behind this program.. the cash position of grain producers and the whole Prairie economy will be substantially improved this fall". I submit that is nonsense. The $6 per acre provided for summerfallow will mostly, if not entirely, be taken up in the cost of additional summerfallow. To suggest this is some kind of cash injection or additional cash in the farmers' pockets is dishonest and misrepresenting what the money will actually have to be used for. It is not-I repeat not-a cash injection of any kind in respect of farm income.
o (5:40 p.m.)
I for one, and the many farmers who have written to me-some of whom have even telephoned and spoken by the hundreds to my colleague the hon. member for Saskatoon-Big-gar in the past several days-resent the inference by any government spokesman and any headline writers of the press that by any means this is an injection of cash into the farmers' pockets, because it is not. Let us put this program in its proper place. All it is is a small carrot and a large club. The small carrot is the $6 an acre payment for converting wheat acreage to summerfallow acreage. A payment of $6 an acre to support the cost of summerfallowing is a mighty small carrot. But the club, or the gun at the head of the farmer, is the new quota system. The farmer who wishes to move a large amount of grain next year must take acreage out of production and must not use that acreage for any crop other than forage.
Whatever misgivings the farmer may have, that the new quota system will persuade him, because he has two choices: it will

either be compulsory, or he has to do it. This new program, operation WARP, is designed to do one thing and one thing only. It is designed to drastically cut wheat production in 1970 without substantially increasing other grain or oilseed crops. On thing it certainly does not do: it does not in any sense relieve the serious cash shortage which has paralyzed the vast majority of grain farmers in Saskatchewan.
Payments under this plan will barely meet costs in the most favourable areas. Certainly, in many areas it will fail to even cover the farmers' costs. Perhaps this program would be tolerable if it were part of a comprehensive attack on the short-term farm crisis and longer term adjustments. But as a minimum it must be accompanied by substantial supplementary payments to farmers related not to next year's production but to this year's lack of income.
Every major farm organization has called for a program of supplementary payments to Prairie grain producers. They have pleaded for this repeatedly over the past several years. It was a central point in the farm program put forward by the members of the official opposition and of my party repeatedly in this House. Possibly in many respects this was as a result of the demand by farm organizations, but in other respects we were putting forward programs which were part of the policies of our respective parties.
We proposed that the federal government provide not less than $200 million to support payments across the three Prairie provinces. Not only did the minister and the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) turn a deaf ear to this proposal, but even the Liberal Premier of Saskatchewan went to the Federal-Provincial Conference in February and made not one demand for supplementary cash payments to meet Saskatchewan's farm crisis. To this day he has failed the farm organizations, the farmers and the small town merchants. His silence and the silence of many other Liberals on this question demonstrates better than anything else the true kinship that exists along the Thateher-Trudeau axis.
We need, first of all, production guides which recognize the value of what farmers can grow as a national trading asset of benefit to all Canada. We need production guides which recognize long-term world food needs. We need production guides which recognize the contribution which satisfying rural life and employment can make to the economic and social structure of Canada. We need,
March 24, 1970

secondly, trade policies to make possible more purchases by people who buy or who would want to buy what we can produce. We have accepted large sales to Russia and China. We accepted these sales as a matter of right. We have done practically nothing about going out and developing the type of trade policies which would solidify, expand or extend these things.
Third, we need government policies in respect of government guarantees. We need government guarantees to buy specified amounts of produce and to buy those specified amounts at prices which will make farming viable and which will encourage people to make it their lifetime work and thereby make possible diversification and other adjustments within the farm industry. What is happening today with regard to diversification is that the farmer is being urged to diversity in the face of excessive costs and a ruinous debt burden, in many cases. The farmer alone is carrying the unfair risk. The government ought to carry some of this responsibility.
We also need laws to prevent the extension of non-farm corporate ownership to larger areas of farm activity. We need laws to establish minimum prices for grain sold within the provinces. The provincial governments can act on this; they can act to establish minimum prices for grain sold within the province. We need laws to fully protect the farmer and others against foreclosure and any other punitive action when, through no fault of his own, he is unable to pay his debts. The farmer will not be able to use the payment of $6 an acre to pay off his debts; he will need this money to buy seed or for summerfallowing.
We need a provincial government, particularly in Saskatchewan, which will support orderly marketing and not attack it as did a Liberal minister in the legislature last month. We need provincial governments which will co-operate and not interfere with the government of Canada when it starts to enforce the necessary laws in respect of orderly marketing. On this score I am pleased that the Minister without Portfolio did not weaken in the face of the opposition he received from his friends in his own province.
Mr. Speaker, I and many members of this House have received many letters, petitions and resolutions either in partial or in complete opposition to, as I call it, operation WARP. I should like to quote from a petition forwarded to the Minister without Portfolio from the Raymore district of Saskatchewan.
Supplementary Estimates It had attached to it the signatures of 104 farmers and small businessmen in that district. The preamble reads:
We, the undersigned farmers in the Raymore area, wish to submit to you the following information for your kind consideration, discussion and positive action:
It goes on to state:
We believe that large wheat inventory is caused by poor distribution. Not overproduction. As long as there is one hungry human in the world we do not wish to cut production. We believe on farm wheat to be an asset, not a liability. We also regard wheat in our granaries as income for the year the wheat was produced, similar to stocks, bonds, cash accumulated by other citizens during previous years of work. No other segment of the population is obliged to opt out of production for twelve months through no fault of its own. No individual, be he the wealthiest man or the poorest, will tell you he can afford to go one whole year without production.
It continues:
The effects of inventory on the farmer as compared to industry differs. If industry decreases its inventory its costs drop almost in direct proportion. In the farmers situation his costs are based on a year's operation. Cost of production per acre changes very little. Yields are affected by variables, not just by value of inputs.
They go on in their petition to cite the reasons they are not in favour of the minister's program. They state:
The proposed plan offers in place of the 1970 wheat crop approximately $100 million as compared to 1969 value of production of $684 million at $1 + = $700 million. Therefore, the plan offers approximately one-seventh of value for the 1970 crop as compared to the 1969 wheat crop which is 15 cents a bushel for 1970 wheat.
They state further:
Storage costs to the federal government will not decrease in proportion to a decreasing stockpile. If we have 450 million bushels stored on the farm, plus 450 million bushels stored in elevators and terminals, or nothing on the farm plus 450 million bushels in elevators, cost of storage will remain the same since the federal government pays storage to the elevator system, not to the farmers.
[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
So there is no saving to the government or to the farmer in storage costs. They contend that the real problem is not one of large inventory but of low sales, low prices, high cost of inputs and high interest rates. They believe-I was particularly struck with this one because I have had similar submissions from people in many parts of the Prairies- that the estimate of the carryover of wheat is too high by at least 20 per cent. I know of substantial areas in Saskatchewan where there is no carryover of wheat. I would like

March 24, 1970
Supplementary Estimates to hear and see the minister's evidence of the 900 million to one billion bushels of wheat that is in farmers' hands and in elevator storage as of July 31. There are six or seven more reasons why these farmers signed this petition. I will read the last one, which says they are opposed to the plan because-
There is no provision for farmers who have no wheat because he was hailed out, dried out, froze out, drowned out, wormed out or craned out-
And I will insert here, "or Liberaled out."
-or the young man trying to start out.
They end their petition by saying:
Therefore, we are opposed to the black paper on wheat reduction program and cannot, and will not, accept its implications.
The Archbishop of the Diocese of Qu'Ap-pelle of the Anglican Church of Canada
wrote:
At the same time we feel strongly that the program to reduce wheat production by the federal government can be regarded only as a means of buying time in which to attack the root problem of food distribution around the world.
We recognize that the decision to limit production of wheat was the only one to make on economic grounds.
Morally, however, it is another matter. When two-thirds of the world population is hungry; when a child dies of hunger every three seconds while food is surplus in western Canada, it seems to us monstrous not to produce food.
I also have here a letter from Avonlea, Saskatchewan, and one from Lancer, Saskatchewan. This brings me to the question: What about next year? My colleague, the hon. member for Saskatoon-Biggar asked that question. I hope the minister will enlighten us some time this evening as to what is to happen next year. A gentleman from Lancer, Saskatchewan, wrote to me as follows:
I have some 500 acres of fallow now and 500 acres of stubble. If I summerfallow the entire amount of 1,000 acres this year, next year I must seed 1,000 acres. I have no choice but to do this because I could not fallow any longer than two years.
So we would like to know from the minister what about next year? I have here another letter from Saskatchewan which says that it is going to be very hard, with no wheat payments this spring, to licence their vehicles, repair their machinery, purchase fuel and cover their day-to-day and monthly living expenses. The writer of the letter is saying this while waiting for the payment of $6 per acre which he is not likely to get by mid-July if he increases his summer fallow. What does

he do for income? As yet they have not delivered their one-bushel quota and their crop year is over half gone.
Some of these letters are copies of ones that I have received. The originals were sent to the minister, and I hope he has read them all carefully. I hope he takes the time to answer the questions put forward by these farmers who have written from various parts of western Canada. One constituent started off his letter by saying:
To pen a letter to me is like a bath to a hippie, however this plan our agricultural department has come up with, namely Lift, has lifted my hand.
The only thing it will lift is a lot of good topsoil and a good many farmers' blood pressure. I can see some merit in this for a farmer who grew only wheat and never tried to reduce his wheat acreage or diversify and was fortunate enough to have a bumper crop every year since 1966. This will certainly help him out, but for people in the Park Belt it is more like a kick in the rear. Mr. Speaker, the motion before the House to concur in interim supply for the period April 1 to June 30 further illustrates the basic conflict which exists within the government. On the one hand we see the western farmer faced with an enormous surplus of wheat for which the government cannot find markets, and in fact through this motion it is asking the House to provide $100 million to pay the western farmer, in effect, not to grow wheat. On the other hand we find the government apparently about to embark on a policy which will further reduce the amount of wheat used for feed grain purposes.
The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Olson) in his estimates has reduced by some $5 million the amount for feed grain assistance for the coming year, and he has given indications that the entire program may be withdrawn. As the House is aware, since 1941 the federal government has paid a subsidy on the transportation of feed grains from the Prairie provinces to the Atlantic provinces and to British Columbia. The program was originally started as a measure to encourage livestock production in those areas where feed grains were in short supply. In effect, the feed grain assistance program was designed to move large amounts of grain from surplus areas to deficit areas.
As the Nova Scotia Federation of Agriculture points out in a recent statement on the program:
With the vast amounts of feed grains on hand in western Canada, it seems to make good economic and common sense to move as much as possible of this surplus grain to eastern Canada and British Columbia, where relatively little grain is produced and feed grain requirements are far from
Supplementary Estimates being met by local production. Furthermore, grain should be produced for livestock feed where the necessary resources are available to produce grain most economically.
This has been the policy since 1941, but from recent statements it would appear that the federal government is now considering the total withdrawal of this assistance program. While it is true that a reduction in the program will mean an immediate saving to the government, any saving obtained will have to be passed on to the farmer in increased costs of production and so will eventually be passed on to the consumer. Here again is the conflict within the government, because this is in direct violation of the government's avowed position of maintaining the line on prices, and it is a direct contradiction of the purpose of the Prices and Incomes Commission that prices should be held down at this time.
The Maritime provinces already suffer from low incomes, and reduction or complete elimination of the feed freight assistance will certainly not help this situation. The Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Mar-chand) has unfurled vast new programs to overcome regional disparities in the Atlantic area, but now we find his colleague proposing measures which will help to negate his efforts. The farmer in the Maritime provinces needs more government help, rather than a reduction in assistance. As the brief from the Nova Scotia Federation of Agriculture points out:
The continuation of the feed freight assistance program can be justified by government and agriculture as an equitable program which gave rise to great development benefits in the past and which contains even greater potentials for the future.
Removal of the program cannot be justified without simultaneously eliminating other restraints such as tariffs on United States grains, Wheat Board import licence requirements and Wheat Board pricing of feed grains so that our livestock feeders can look to other areas of the continent for a supply of feed grains at the lowest possible cost.
[DOT] (8:10 p.m.)
I think the federation is saying, in effect, that if the government does not want Maritime farmers to use western feed grains because they have suddenly found some market for those grains, then take off the other restrictions so that the Maritime farmers can buy feed grains from other sources. I hope the minister will take this into consideration. This action of the government is only

March 24, 1970
Supplementary Estimates another roadblock in our fight to obtain a comprehensive transportation policy for the Atlantic provinces.
It is an historical fact that because the Maritime provinces are situated at such great distances from the markets of central Canada, special freight rate assistance must be given to them so they can compete with other parts of the country. What is particularly disturbing to every Maritimer is the fact that for almost three years now the region has been in a kind of suspended animation interrupted occasionally by announcements from various transport ministers-and we have had quite a few-that a rational and sound transportation policy was being worked out for the area, and disturbed at other intervals by various railway freight increases.
We have had commissions and committees studying the problem, but as yet they have not come up with any solutions. The Transport Committee has made two trips to the region, and almost a year ago now presented a very comprehensive report containing their suggestions for a new transportation policy. The Atlantic Premiers presented an excellent report about a year ago and made many suggestions which would go a long way toward solving some of our problems.
In November, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Jamieson) announced the formation of a new federal-provincial committee on Atlantic region transportation, and included in its terms of reference was to be a detailed examination of the Maritime freight rate assistance on rail traffic within the region. This committee was composed of representatives from each of the Atlantic provinces, with a federal appointee to act as chairman. We have been told by the minister the committee has met four times, and I am informed that they have agreed on two recommendations. These recommendations refer to two noticeable errors in the Atlantic Regional Freight Assistance Act passed in this House in the last year. This is the only concrete step that has been taken in some three years under three different ministers of transport to revise the Maritime Freight Rates Act.
Because the Maritime Freight Rates Act has sometimes been deliberately misconstrued and misinterpreted, we have been accused of asking for things to which we are not entitled. For a moment or two I should like to refer to the background of this legislation. When this act was passed in 1927 it was a direct result of the recommendations made by the Royal Commission on Maritime Claims,

commonly known as the Duncan Commission, appointed in 1926 to study the problems of freight rates in the area as compared with the rest of Canada.
The findings were very interesting because the study indicated that between 1912 and 1925 freight rates in the area had increased by 92 per cent, while rates elsewhere in Canada had increased by only 55 per cent. As the commission pointed out, this high increase placed a burden upon the trade and commerce in the region and, in fact, made it almost impossible for business to compete in the Canadian market.
The point that I want to make, because it has been deliberately overlooked, is that to adjust this discrepancy the Duncan Commission recommended that there be an immediate 20 per cent decrease in rates in the Maritime area. In other words, the 20 per cent decrease that is sneeringly referred to as the maritime subsidy is nothing more than this recommendation which was to bring our rate back to the same level that applied in the rest of the country. This interpretation is very irritating to people in the Maritime provinces.
The Maritime Freight Rates Act has served its purpose in some cases, but it certainly could not be called a rousing success nor an abject failure. It has helped business and commerce in the area, but it has not fulfilled the original intention of preventing rail rates there increasing more than in the rest of Canada. It has not kept transportation costs from being a barrier to the marketing of goods from the region throughout the country.
The philosophy in the act was good, but somewhere along the line the mechanics failed. To show what has happened in the erosion of our competitive position as compared with 1927, when the next round of railway freight rate increases come into effect on April 6 the rates will have caught up with three of the four rate hikes applied across the country which have meant increases of 20 per cent to 38 per cent in various categories since the National Transportation Act became effective on March 23, 1967. The Atlantic region will have had increases of 14 per cent to 28 per cent since September 23, 1969. In other words, the 20 per cent laid down by statute in the Maritime Freight Rates Act has gone out the window.
The only step the government has taken to implement the intent of the National Transportation Act, which was to develop a transportation policy for all modes of transportation in Canada, has been to pass Bill C-207, the
March 24, 1970

Atlantic Regional Freight Assistance Act. This bill was supposed to extend the same assistance to truckers as that extended to rail carriers, but those who drafted it did a sloppy job and created the two inequities which are causing further confusion in the Maritime freight rates picture.
[DOT] (8:20 p.m.)
Two errors appeared in the drafting of the legislation which extended these subsidies to the truckers in the area. The subsidies were supposed to be comparable to those granted to rail carriers. By some quirk or error in the drafting of the legislation it turned out that the subsidy on the westward movement of freight was extended to household goods; in other words, furniture. The trucker hauling furniture for someone moving from the Mari-times to another part of Canada can collect a subsidy on the shipment. In other words, we are paying for the migration of maritimers. The second problem is that because different methods are used to compute the amount of assistance, the assistance paid can be substantially less for goods moved by truck than for the same type of shipment by rail.
The Saint John Telegraph-Journal had this to say about the matter:
-in one category, a wide range of miscellaneous commodities in lots of 1,500 pounds or more, the rate by both truck and railway piggyback service is 99 cents per 100 pounds-but because of the different formulas under the two acts, the subsidy works out at 21 cents by truck and 26 cents by rail.
I am talking about the act the Minister of Transport introduced in the House with such flowery promises. The railways were to have no real advantage over the truckers. How the minister's draftsmen produced this mess, we shall never know. We simply must amend the act. The provision extending a subsidy to the movement of household goods must be corrected as soon as possible, before too many people move themselves and their furniture out of the Atlantic area.
The editorial in the Telegraph-Journal continues as follows:
-the disparity between truck and rail subsidies would not have arisen if Ottawa had followed the recommendation of the Atlantic Premiers, based on the extensive task force study, that the subsidies be paid directly to the shippers instead of to the carriers. Such a system would also permit a desirable flexibility in using the assistance, and it would spur rather than dull the competition for traffic between railways and truckers.
The editorial deals with one of the most serious complaints that I and other members 21774-661
Supplementary Estimates from the Atlantic provinces have against the whole approach displayed by the department and the Minister of Transport toward the problem of transportation in the Maritimes. The minister asked for advice from various sources. He asked the Atlantic Premiers for their recommendations and said he would consider them seriously. The Atlantic premiers submitted a comprehensive report containing excellent suggestions. The suggestions respecting the solutions to our problems have all been accepted by most shippers in the area. I suppose we shall discover that this report has been tossed under a desk somewhere and completely ignored.
The minister said he would appoint a federal-provincial committee to look into this question: why, I do not know, because he already had received the report of the Premiers. Why would he wish to appoint a committee? I can only suspect the reason, as can the people of my area. The minister must want further delay. The committee has met four times, and its chairman is a federal appointee. The question is, why cannot the Minister of Transport obtain a report from the committee? Is it any wonder the people of the area are accusing the minister and this government of deliberate heel-dragging on the promise to develop a new Atlantic transportation policy?

Our problems would be solved, the shippers in the Atlantic area would be governed by a definite policy and everything in the area would be fine.

I do not know whether it is primarily the responsibility of the Minister of Fisheries, or the President of the Treasury Board-I suspect it is more the result of the actions of the latter-that we appear here to be involved in a situation where we are robbing Peter to pay Paul. This is something to which I strongly object.
It is all very well for the government to announce great programs to reimburse fishermen for loss because of pollution, or to announce grants to bolster the price that fishermen will receive for their fish through the support board, as if these were great programs and we were being asked to approve the funds to carry them out, but let us not blind ourselves to the fact that what appears to be happening is that in order to do this we are taking away from certain other very important aspects of public spending.
These are items referred to in the main estimates. The one that concerns me is vote No. 10 in the main estimates which has to do with fisheries management and development programs, including moneys for the construction or acquisition of buildings, works, land and equipment including acquisition of land for the International Pacific Salmon Fisheries Commission as required by article VIII of the convention, and payments to provinces or municipalities. The item goes on about details of the industrial development service, conservation and protect'on service, resource development service and inspection service.
My quarrel with what is happening here is that at a time when there is a crying need for expansion in the resource development aspect of the Department of Fisheries, the government is, willingly or unwillingly, taking from the Minister of Fisheries and Forestry and his

Supplementary Estimates department moneys that Parliament in good faith appropriated to carry out certain purposes, particularly resource development, and is shifting that money to what may be worthy objects in themselves but certainly are not the objects for which we originally intended the money to be used when we voted it. The Minister of Fisheries was in British Columbia quite recently to speak to the annual convention of the largest organization of fishermen in that province. I do not know whether the President of the Treasury Board is going to take advantage of this opportunity to deal with some of the questions that have been raised today, but if he does I hope this will be one aspect of the proposal before us with which he is prepared to come to grips. At the outset I should like to refer to the report and tell you, Mr. Speaker, what we are talking about and what, for the sake of $30 million or $40 million a year, this government has thrown down the drain. Therefore, I have no hesitation in saying, on behalf of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, what's $30 million or $40 million when dealing with the lives of two or three million people and offering them the wherewithal to get out from under the yoke of criticism from Ontario and Quebec to
