the effect that they are saddled with the burden of subsidies for the Atlantic provinces?
I want to be serious because we are dealing with public money, and I hope I can keep in order with what I wish to say tonight. For two years I have been asking about the feasibility study. Your Honour knows my concern about it. God knows, it has been my dream for 20 years that I would see these tides harnessed, and I shall not rest until they are. I shall read one short paragraph from page 14 of the report:
In the United States the total requirements of the six New England States in 1965 were 41,782 million KWH of energy with a peak demand of 8,586 MW. The requirements are forecast to increase to 111,000 million KWH and over 22,000 MW by 1980, and to approximately 210,000 million KWH and 41,000 MW in 1990.
The foregoing predictions indicate the tremendous increases in generating capacity for which planning must be carried out in the northeastern region of the continent. Also evident is the fact that, from the standpoint of magnitude of requirement, there is a market for the disposal of large quantities of energy from any conceivable size of electric power development.
In this world there is only one source of energy which can meet that type of requirement, and we happen to have it in the provinces of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick. It seems to me the government of Canada has adopted a shockingly short-term view in its decision not to proceed with the exploitation of the tremendous potential energy of the Bay of Fundy and Minas Basin tidal power. For over two years many of us have been anxiously awaiting this report. We have been concerned about the economic well-being of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick. I do not say that loosely, nor do I say it unadvisedly.
I say that the decision not to go ahead with the project because, as the report indicates, the cost of money is too high, is shortsighted. As the report says, the cost per kilowatt hour is beyond the range of industry to absorb. We are not unmindful of that. We know that an industry must have cheap power to keep it competitive with other industries. We know we cannot have power that will cost one mill or two mills more than power produced thermally or by some other means.
What we are talking about is the cost of being Canadian-and I want to pay that price. I do not know whether the rest of the members in the House want to pay it. I was prepared to pay it in terms of the St. Lawrence Seaway. Now I ask the rest of Canada to at least have second thoughts about the decision of the government not to go ahead with the development of this power.
As I said, this is one of the government's most shortsighted conclusions because it overlooks three major factors. The first is the potentiality of tidal power to meet energy requirements free of consequential pollution and at a constant, fixed cost once the capital requirement has been met. It would be pollution-free and constant in terms of the cost factor of annual operations. No other form of production of electrical energy provides that. Tidal power does provide it because it is

March 24, 1970
Supplementary Estimates constant, it is renewable and we could use it four times a day. Four times a day, 135 billion cubic feet of water moves in and out of the bay. All we have to do is to utilize the optimum effect and subsidize the cost of money.
There seems to be concern for the cost of capital during the period of construction, which is predicted to be nine years. I will bet you a dollar that I could find a dozen conglomerates or consortiums in this field that would guarantee they would have an operation in six to seven years, not nine years. I ask the House, the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Drury) and the government to consider the very simple proposition, within the concept of regional economic expansion and within what I know is a sincere desire on the part of the government to overcome disparity, to make Canada a whole unit in which each part feels as strong as the others-because truth is never what it is; more often it is what it seems to be. I ask the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the government if they would not reconsider the blunt statement made by the Prime Minister yesterday not to go ahead with this project.
I have mentioned the power that will be required in this section of Canada and the northeastern United States by 1980 and by 1990. No amount of thermal energy or nuclear energy will meet that demand unless we pay the price in terms of pollution, and not only pollution of our air in terms of coaldust and oil getting into the atmosphere but other forms of pollution. I ask the President of the Treasury Board where we will bury uranium in 1985, the uranium that they use to boil water to generate electricity in nuclear plants.
The U.S.A. are now down to two small areas, one in the mid-southwest and one in Alaska, where they can put away uranium which has a half life of 5,000 years, or whatever it is. I am not sure what it is today. I do not want it in Nova Scotia. Does the President of the Treasury Board want it in his backyard? I bet him a buck that he does not,

yet here we are thoughtlessly casting aside another source of power because we are afraid of the cost of money.
The price of the power per kilowatt hour will bring it beyond competitive range. How shortsighted we are: I ask the President of the Treasury Board how many hours he has spent talking about pollution at cabinet meetings. The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Greene) is one of the finest men in this country but, good God, how can he stand up after hours and hours of conversation about pollution and say, "Let us build more thermal power plants. Let us pollute more air"? What are we talking about?
The short-range project is fine, because we will need more energy and more electrical power before we can tie into an international or national grid the power of the tides of the Bay of Fundy. Let us not bog down in the concept that we can simply shelve it until the interest rate comes down to 5 per cent. I pray God I should live so long, but I do not think it will ever be that low again. How can it? There is no hope for it since the Bank Act revision.
We cannot continue this type of philosophy. The report says that the construction will take nine years in its optimum arrangement, to utilize the tides going both ways. I am not sure what engineering principles are involved, but they say it will cost $724 million plus. Basing it on the 1968 rate of 7 per cent, it will be "X" dollars and it will put the mill price per kilowatt hour at "X" level. Even if, realistically speaking, the interest rate today is 10 per cent and will continue to be that over the nine-year period, which I indicated will not be that long, and even if the cost is so high, in order to bring it down to a competitive level some sacrifice will be required of all Canadians.
[DOT] (9:20 p.m.)
The government talks about the need for Canadians to make sacrifices. How long have we been paying for the St. Lawrence Seaway? It still cannot pay its debt out of operational cash flow. I suggested in this House three, four or maybe five years ago that we should extend the write-off period for the St. Lawrence Seaway to 75 years, in the hope that operational cash flow might begin to meet its debt retirement obligations.
I am suggesting that for a period of six or seven years we should subsidize the cost of money to enable us to reach a competitive level. Let us pay that simple price as Canadi-
March 24, 1970

ans. Let us do it and not be too concerned about what we are doing. Let us look at it in terms of the subsidies that have been poured into the Atlantic region, particularly Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, in years past, and which will have to be poured into it in future years until we build the market that will attract manufacturing industries.
Once the project is built, let us subsidize the cost of money over and above the competitive level, up to the point where the price per kilowatt here is competitive. In other words, let us tap the American market. Let us benefit the people of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick with massive, cheap energy the like of which has not been conceived in Canada previously. Mr. Speaker, where have you ever seen a report dealing so casually with billions of kilowatt hours? You have not seen any other and you will not see any other, because this situation exists nowhere in North America except the Bay of Fundy. We are shortsighted in not going ahead with this project. We are doing ourselves and Canada a disservice. The failure to go ahead with it now does not mean we will not have to go ahead with it in the future. We will have to go ahead with it in the future. We will have to go ahead with the development within the next decade, because we do not have any other sources of energy.
I have talked about pollution. If we do not think pollution is important, the message has not got through from the government down to the grass roots. It got through to me, Mr. Speaker, and I am aware of it. I do my laundry at home, and I do not buy the type of detergent about which the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mrs. Maclnnis) talks; I buy the other stuff that does not have a pollutant in it. Much as we need electric energy, I cannot conceive of supporting any project that would spread pollution. I say that we should consider the stable cost factor that is represented by Minas Basin tidal power.
I quote recommendation No. 5, which is to be found at page 22 of the board's report, as follows:
The board recommends further that additional detailed studies be authorized when (a) the interest rate on money drops sufficiently to suggest the possibility of an economic tidal power development in the Bay of Fundy-
In all seriousness, Mr. Speaker, when is that going to be? Who is kidding whom? These 22 pages were designed to justify a no. I think that the whole 2J feet thickness of study papers and working papers should be
Supplementary Estimates referred to an independent, outside agency or body for review, particularly as they apply to the cost of money. I continue the quotation:
- (b) a major breakthrough in construction costs or in the cost of generating equipment suggests the possibility of designing an economic tidal power development in the Bay of Fundy-
We can wait forever for the sun to shine on Ottawa and the temperature to be 70 degrees all year. That is a bland comment. How will we evolve cheaper methods of developing tidal power unless we get into the business of designing equipment to capitalize on tidal power?

Mr. Speaker, I would like to bring to your attention a chain of events which has taken place in the last few weeks and which has had a profound effect on the town of Elliot Lake in my riding. I have just returned from a series of urgent meetings with people who are involved in that community-the town council, the leaders of the labour unions, the businessmen's associations and the other people.
A few weeks ago the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) announced that the government had become aware that there were negotiations taking place between the Roman Corporation and the Hudson's Bay Company to sell the controlling interest in Denison Mines to that company, and he indicated that the government would move to block this sale, if necessary with retroactive legislation, because the Hudson's Bay Company was controlled by American interests.
A subsequent meeting between the Prime Minister and Mr. Roman seemed to end on a very amicable note with Mr. Roman indicating that the Prime Minister's approach was fair. At the same time there seemed to be an indication in statements by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Greene) that arrangements could be worked out which would allow the government's policy on foreign ownership to be maintained and yet allow Mr. Roman to make his sale. However, last Thursday night the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources announced the details of the government's rules for foreign ownership and indicated that Canadian mining companies would have to have Canadian ownership of 66 per cent, with no individual foreign owner holding more than 10 per cent.

March 24, 1970
Supplementary Estimates
Last Friday morning Mr. Roman held a press conference in Toronto. I would like to read the news report which came out of that conference, as follows:
Denison Mines Ltd. may consider closing Its huge uranium mine at Elliot Lake, Ontario, for three or four years if additional financial resources cannot be negotiated soon.
The chairman of Denison Mines, Stephen B. Roman, told a Toronto news conference today "without additional resources management definitely has to give consideration to closing the mines."
Mr. Roman had originally called the news conference to announce details of a sale of about one quarter of Denison stock to a U.S. controlled corporation.
He used it instead to comment on government restrictions announced last night, that apparently would block the deal.
Mr. Roman said he could not comment on his next step until the government's action had been thoroughly studied. He said many points were left open in the statement by Energy Minister, J. J. Greene, and he added "if possible I definitely will go through with the deal."
This news hit the town of Elliot Lake like a bombshell. Mr. Speaker, this town has been through some very bad years. When the American options to purchase uranium were not picked up in the early sixties, the town went from a boom to a bust situation. We had homes and businesses closed and fortunes lost. Fortunately, the government had introduced a stockpiling program in 1963 and a further one in 1965 which, incidentally, will be terminated on June 30 of this year.
[DOT] (9:30 p.m.)
In 1966 things started to pick up. Businesses reopened, homes started to sell and building commenced. During this period the government has poured upward of $100 million into the stockpiling program, which was utilized by the Denison Corporation. Though this program ends on June 30, Mr. Roman has indicated that he has enough uranium on hand to meet all his contractual commitments for the next three years and that he could close the mine and still meet his commitments for this period.
This may well be true, Mr. Speaker, but I say Mr. Roman has a responsibility to the town as well as to his board of directors. The town has been responsible for good things in his life, and he should now act responsibly toward the community. At the same time, I think the federal government has a responsibility to keep the mine open. They have already poured millions into the stockpiling program and if they allow the mine to close

they will be faced with a terrific welfare expense, as well as moving expenses for the miners for the next three years.
All indications are that world demand for uranium will greatly increase and that the mine will have to remain open. Indeed, Denison Mines closed a contract in the last couple of months with Japanese interests for something like $300 million. I say the government has a responsibility to take whatever action is necessary to see that this mine is kept operating and that the miners do not suffer hardship and unemployment.

Mr. Speaker, in the few moments left at my disposal I should like to confine my remarks to the supplementary estimates before the House, with particular reference to those dealing with agriculture which represent approximately half the total estimates.
I should like to divide my remarks into two headings. First, the method by which this scheme is being introduced and, second, the principle behind the issue. First let us deal with the method. In common with many members, regardless on which side of the House they may sit, I do not like to see legislation brought in by means of estimates. The practice of making statutory changes by way of appropriation acts based on supplementary estimates is no way to bring in legislation. The importance of the disbursement of money to farmers as an incentive not to grow wheat is important enough for a piece of legislation or a bill to be introduced in this House.
Dealing with the method, let us look at the estimates and see what is said. This money is to establish a reserve of:
$100 million from which payments may be made in the fiscal year 1970-71 for wheat acreage reduction of $6 per acre.
I do not find any mention of $10 an acre for seeding into grass.
-in respect of such acreage as may be further prescribed by the Governor in Council-
Of course, the Governor in Council can prescribe whatever they like; Members of Parliament have no control over the matter.
-in accordance with the terms and conditions approved by the Governor in Council to farmers-
It goes on to say, prescribed by the executive or Order in Council. I am saying that this amount of money should have been granted by means of legislation. Another thing I object to is that on the front page it says that these estimates are for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1970. That is the end of this month.
March 24. 1970

We are asked to approve $100 million for this purpose, but the money is to be spent in the year 1970-71. This is an extremely bad practice.

subtopic: BUSINESS OF SUPPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: BUSINESS OF SUPPLY
speechtext:
It is bad practice to be passing money this year which will be spent next year although it appears in this year's estimates. It should appear in next year's estimates, not last year's. It is a very bad precedent and a bad method that the government has chosen to have this $100 million appropriated.
While on the matter of estimates under agriculture, I see that there are three $1 votes here. This is a very dangerous way to pass estimates. Hon. members do not know what that $1 is for, and there is nothing here to explain it. I say again, Mr. Speaker, that I am definitely opposed to the way the government has chosen to get this $100 million from the Consolidated Revenue Fund.
Let us talk about the principle of giving $100 million to the farmers to sit and do nothing. This does not meet with my approval at all, and for the life of me I cannot see why an agricultural country such as Canada should have to do such a thing. By the time the money is administered and an army of people are hired to see that the program is conducted according to the regulations, about $200 million of government money will have been spent. Would it not have been better to buy $200 million worth of wheat from western farmers and ship it to starving people in other parts of the world?

subtopic: BUSINESS OF SUPPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: BUSINESS OF SUPPLY
speechtext:
Surely, that would have made more sense than to pay farmers not to produce it. Also, our image throughout the world would not have suffered. Just this morning I heard of a missionary recently returned from India where there are thousands of hungry and starving people. He said that the news is getting to them that Canada is paying its farmers not to produce wheat, and he asks, "How can I go back to India and face these people, as a Canadian?"
This is a paradoxical situation. We have spent millions and millions of dollars on the Department of Agriculture, we have had experimental farms, we have a department of agriculture in every province, agricultural colleges all over the country, we pay civil servants, research people and others to produce a policy of foresight and vision so that
Supplementary Estimates we will not find ourselves in this position in Canada. What do we find? We find that beef in Canada is at its highest price since the war days. We know children are going to bed in Canada without having had a good meal of red-blooded, high-protein meat. Why is this, Mr. Speaker? It is because the price of beef is so high that the average family cannot afford to buy it for its children.
[DOT] (9:40 p.m.)
There are piles of wheat in western Canada and we do not know what to do with it, yet beef is so highly priced that few can afford to buy it. How foolish can we be? What have all the departmental researchers been doing? Why did they not provide us with a policy that would have averted this situation? Why was no foresight displayed? We live in an agricultural country but import every year about nine pounds of meat per capita. We import lamb, mutton, pork and even beef from other countries of the world, yet at the same time wheat is piling up in Canada. Is that not a strange paradox for this country?
I know some will say that this government should have adopted certain policies. Perhaps that is so, to a certain extent. I think the researchers of the various departments should have told us what policies to adopt in order to avoid our present situation. To anyone who says that the government ought to be the guiding star in presenting policies, I say, "If Alvin Hamilton had been minister of agriculture during these past years, farmers in western Canada would not have been growing so much wheat. They would have seeded to pastures and carrying on a cow-calf program. As a result, more cattle would have been produced and hopefully the price of beef would be low enough for every Canadian to afford it.
Now the government is asking this House to vote $100 million and get it out of this mess. Instead of introducing this measure as a vote in the estimates, the government ought to have introduced a bill which hon. members could debate. That way we might all understand what is to happen in western Canada. As I said before, these estimates apply to 1969-70 but the money will be spent in the period 1970-71.
I shall finish on this note, Mr. Speaker. Some of the best research people live in our country. If they put their minds to it, they can work wonders. Surely, wheat in this country can be used for purposes other than animal and human consumption. For all I know, it might be possible to make silk stock-

Alcohol was distilled from the potato and was ultimately used to drive their vehicles. Yet in this country we sit on mountains of wheat and cannot find a use for it. We tell our farmers not to grow more wheat. How foolish can we be?
